new_en: 17) A convert joins a minyan of 10 for every davar shebikdushah. Although we say, "I shall be sanctified among the Children of Israel," and Tosafot, Sukkah 28b, s.v. Lerabot, state that the expression "Children of Israel" excludes converts unless there is an inclusion, here the verse is only an asmachta. A convert is fit to serve as shaliach tzibbur, as stated in siman 53, seif 19, and there is no reason that he should not join the 10. Pri Megadim there. Pithei HaDevir, letter 1, writes likewise; see there. Levushei Serad on Magen Avraham, seif katan 7, also writes so. A convert who underwent brit milah but has not immersed does not join until he immerses. Siddur Beit Yaakov, laws of Kaddish, letter 16, in the name of Responsa Radbaz, part 3, siman 478, Furth edition.

20) Regarding the Kaddish recited by orphans, according to the Arizal it is specifically the final Kaddish recited before Aleinu that benefits the soul of the deceased. Shaar HaKavanos, discourse concerning Kaddish, writes: "The final Kaddish is not included among the ordinary Kaddishim, because all the realms have already ascended. This Kaddish is called Kaddish Yasom, meaning the Kaddish recited by orphans. The matter is that this Kaddish pertains to Asiyah, where there is the aspect of death, in order to elevate all the souls and nefashot in the secret of resurrection. Therefore orphans recite it upon the death of a father or mother," etc. See what we wrote above in letter 1 in the name of Torat Chacham.

"It appears to me that I heard from my teacher that it is proper to recite this Kaddish for the death of one's father or mother throughout the entire year, even on Shabbos and Yom Tov. The reason is not, as the masses think, merely that it helps save the deceased's soul from the judgment of Gehinnom. It has another benefit: bringing the soul into Gan Eden and elevating it from level to level. Accordingly, it should be recited even on Shabbos and Yom Tov. I saw my teacher recite the final Kaddish every year on the day his father died, at all 3 prayers." End quote.

Thus, according to the Rav, the Kaddish that benefits the soul of the deceased is specifically the final Kaddish. Here in our holy city of Jerusalem, may it be built and established, some have the custom that orphans also recite the Kaddish before Hodu and the Kaddish before Kaveh, while all the other Kaddishim are recited by the chazzan alone. It appears to me that the reason they also recite these 2 Kaddishim is that they correspond to the ascent of Asiyah, the aspect of nefesh, into Yetzirah, and it is possible that they likewise benefit the nefesh of the deceased.

All this applies to the seudah hamafseket when one does not intend to eat another fixed meal afterward and the meal is after halachic noon. But if it is before halachic noon, or it is after halachic noon and he intends to eat another fixed meal afterward, he need not observe these restrictions. {Rama: The custom throughout the regions of Ashkenaz is to eat a fixed meal before Minchah, then pray Minchah, and afterward eat the seudah hamafseket. [Maharil] The custom is to increase somewhat at the first meal so that the fast will not harm them, since they stop eating while it is still day, as on Yom Kippur. There is some support for this from Midrash Eichah Rabbati. Nevertheless, one who is able to afflict himself, knows that the fast will not harm him, and is stringent upon himself is called holy, as appears to me.}

"To young children." Bach writes that the wine should be given to the infant receiving brit milah, as stated in siman 621, seif 3, regarding Yom Kippur. Rama, however, holds that since Tisha B'Av is rabbinic, we are not so stringent, and it is preferable to give it to a somewhat older child who is obligated in chinuch for the blessing. Magen Avraham.

"To children." We are not concerned that they may become accustomed to doing so, as stated in siman 556, because this does not occur every year. [Tur] Bach writes that the wine should be given to the infant receiving brit milah, as stated in siman 621, seif 3, regarding Yom Kippur. Rama, however, holds that since Tisha B'Av is rabbinic, we are not so stringent. It is preferable to give it to a somewhat older child who is obligated in chinuch for the blessing, as stated in siman 269.

If there is an infant who must receive brit milah, the brit milah is performed after the kinot are completed. Some wait to perform it until after halachic noon. The blessing over the brit milah is recited without spices. The custom follows the first view. If the mother who gave birth is present at the place of the brit milah, the blessing is recited over a cup and she drinks from it, provided that she hears the blessing and does not interrupt by speaking between hearing the blessing and drinking from the cup. If she is not there, the blessing is recited over the cup and children are given a taste from it.
"There, where it is possible that it will be rebuilt." For Tosafot explicitly explained it this way in Bava Basra 60b.

The law of accepting a fast, containing 13 seifim. Any fast upon which the sun did not set, meaning that he did not complete it until tzeit hakochavim, is not considered a fast. Tzeit hakochavim here means that 3 medium-sized stars are visible, or that the moon shines strongly enough to illuminate the earth. If he intends to eat before then, he does not recite Aneinu. {Rama: Nevertheless, some have the custom to recite Aneinu even when they do not complete the fast until tzeit hakochavim, in accordance with some authorities. [Terumat HaDeshen, siman 157] It appears to me that this applies specifically to an individual, who says Aneinu in Shomea Tefillah, since he may in any event add personal supplications there, as explained above in siman 119. A shaliach tzibbur, however, should not recite Aneinu unless the fast is completed, and this is the custom.}

There in Magen Avraham, seif katan 16: "It is strained to distinguish." In my humble opinion, although regarding charity the Mechaber rules like Maharam cited by Mordechai, nevertheless regarding a fast Maharam must agree that the law is different, whether one derives this from reasoning or from the Gemara.

By reasoning: Mordechai's rationale is that a verbal declaration to Heaven is like delivery to an ordinary person, and an asmachta can likewise take effect in certain dealings between people; see Sema, siman 207, seif katan 56. This explains a vow to give an object to sacred use, because there exists a corresponding form of acquisition that can take effect between ordinary people. A vow to fast, however, has no comparable acquisition between ordinary people. In such a matter there is no basis to say that an asmachta takes effect merely because the declaration was directed to Heaven.

The Gemara likewise supports this. In the relevant passages concerning vows and conditional undertakings, a distinction emerges between a commitment involving property that can be transferred or consecrated and a personal undertaking such as fasting. A property commitment can take effect through the special force of a declaration to Heaven, whereas a conditional personal undertaking remains subject to the ordinary law of asmachta.

Accordingly, the Mechaber's conclusion concerning one who says, "If God saves me from this distress," need not follow Mordechai's principle. Mordechai in Bava Kamma brings proof from Yaakov's statement, "If God will be with me," as cited in Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat. If Maharam held that every vow undertaken in a time of distress becomes binding because of the rationale recorded by Magen Avraham, there would be no proof from Yaakov that asmachta generally takes effect. The same is true of the verse, "If You will indeed deliver this people into my hand, I will devote their cities": there the commitment concerned devotion of property to sacred use, where the declaration itself has the force of transfer.

It must therefore be that Maharam does not accept the broad rationale stated by Magen Avraham here. Once we have established that asmachta applies fully to a vow to fast, even a vow made in a time of distress does not automatically become binding according to Mordechai. Beit Yosef records here a stringent view of R' Yehonatan, but Mordechai's own principle does not prove such a stringency for fasting.

Yaakov's vow, "If God will be with me," concerned making the stone a house of God and tithing everything God would give him. Those are property commitments to Heaven and therefore take effect by the special rule of a declaration to Heaven. Likewise, "If You will indeed deliver this people" concerns devoting the cities, again a commitment of property to sacred use. There is therefore no proof from either verse concerning a conditional fast.

With this, the difficulty of Taz, seif katan 17, is resolved. See Mordechai, chapter Shor Shenagach 4 and 5, siman 44; Nekudat HaKesef, Yoreh De'ah, siman 258; and Nimukei Yosef, chapter Mi SheMet, on the Mishnah concerning one who says that if his wife bears a male child he shall receive 1 maneh. Examine all this carefully.

(48) "And a compulsory fast occurred among them." This applies even if, when he made his vow, he did not say "these days," but merely accepted upon himself to fast 40 consecutive days beginning today.

(49) "They count for him." This applies specifically to a compulsory fast that did not arise through a vow. If he already had a fasting obligation through a vow, for example he vowed to fast every Monday and Thursday and afterward vowed to fast 40 consecutive days, the Monday and Thursday fasts do not count toward the 40, because these are 2 separate vows, unless he explicitly states that he intends them to be included in the count of 40.

Nevertheless, one who had already been accustomed to fast during the 10 Days of Repentance, which is itself similar to a vow, and afterward, on 15 Av, vowed to fast 40 consecutive days, may count the 10 Days of Repentance within the 40. His clear intent is to parallel the 40 days during which Moshe ascended the mountain, as stated in seif 4, and it is therefore as though he explicitly said "these 40 days." It is obvious that even if several obligatory fasts occur during them, they count toward his total.

One who is accustomed to fast the 10 Days of Repentance and whose father's yahrzeit falls between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur need not add another fast before Rosh Hashanah on account of that day, just as Tzom Gedaliah and Yom Kippur are obligatory yet count among the 10 days. If his father's yahrzeit falls before Rosh Hashanah during the Selichot period, he must fast 4 additional days besides that yahrzeit. If the yahrzeit falls on the first day of Selichot or on Erev Rosh Hashanah, he need not fast a different day in its place, because those days are permanently included in the established group of 10 fasting days.

"So as not to cause prices to rise." When people see that 2 large meals are being purchased, 1 for the evening and 1 for Shabbos, they may think that famine has come and raise prices.

"Where there is no concern for this." For example, in a city whose majority are non-Jews. It is possible that in these countries, where people who artificially raise prices are uncommon, a fast may be decreed on Thursday, and this is the custom.

If rains become so excessive that they muddy the ground and prevent plowing, how should one act? This siman contains 1 seif. In every place, if excessive rains muddy the ground and prevent plowing, they sound an alarm and plead for mercy. If the matter is urgent and there is no time to follow the ordinary sequence of communal fasts, they do not impose a communal fast upon the congregation, because the congregation cannot fast every day. Rather, they sound the alarm every day and at every prayer, and they cry out verbally in their distress: "Our Father, answer us." They say: "May it be Your will before You, Hashem our God and God of our fathers, that Your mercy subdue Your anger, that Your mercy prevail over Your attributes, that You deal with Your children through the attribute of mercy and enter for them beyond the strict line of judgment. In Your great goodness have mercy upon them, for punishment comes upon the earth only because of Israel, and they are Your people and Your inheritance whom You brought out of Egypt. They are unable to bear either an excess of evil or an excess of good. You bestowed much good upon them and they could not bear it; You became angry with them and they could not bear it. May it be Your will that there be relief upon the earth, and remember Your mercies."

"There." This applies even to what he concludes at the end concerning bowing, except that those precise in pronunciation, etc. The word "verish'ah" should be pronounced with a chirik under the resh and a sheva under the shin. This is the correct reading.

"They perform brit milah." Taz writes: I heard that the Gaon Moreinu HaRav Rabbi Feivish of Krakow performed a brit milah on Rosh Hashanah and did not wipe his mouth after the procedure; rather, while his mouth was still soiled with the blood of the brit milah, he blew the shofar, in order to combine the mitzvah of brit milah with the mitzvah of shofar.

When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos, the piyyut Zechor Brit is not recited; the brit milah is performed after Ashrei, and Yom LaYabashah is recited. On a weekday the piyyut is recited and Yom LaYabashah is not recited. The same applies on every Yom Tov. Magen Avraham. See Levush, and see siman 490, seif 7, regarding what is written there.
